Nottingham Forest vs. Chelsea: How to watch, date, time, live stream and TV channel for Premier League clash

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (394 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 13:37.
  • Nottingham Forest and Chelsea will attempt to earn a much-needed boost in the Premier League when they square off on Friday night.
  • Despite seven points separating these teams in the Premier League table, the home side are arguably the favourites to prevail from this fixture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 13:37.

Nottingham Forest and Chelsea will attempt to earn a much-needed boost in the Premier League when they square off on Friday night.

Despite seven points separating these teams in the Premier League table, the home side are arguably the favourites to prevail from this fixture.

Here, Sports Mole provides details of how to tune into the contest.

The Premier League match will kick off at 8pm, UK time, on Saturday.

This Premier League game between Nottingham Forest and Chelsea will be held at the City Ground, the home stadium of Forest.

Last season's corresponding fixture ended in a 3-0 victory for Chelsea, albeit in a game where Forest - then with Ange Postecoglou at the helm - squandered a number of opportunities.

The Premier League contest will be available on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Premier League for viewers in the UK.

Sky customers can access the Premier League match on Sky Go and on the Sky Sports app, while it is also available via Now TV's Sports membership.

Sky Sports will show highlights, including any goals which have been scored, on their social media and YouTube channels, as well as on their dedicated app.

Meanwhile, those wishing to watch highlights on Match of the Day will have to wait until Saturday evening, with the programme starting at 10.30pm.

Both teams head into this fixture with question marks over their physicality, an issue which Oliver Glasner addressed in his pre-match press conference.

Forest begin the latest batch of games sitting in 17th position in the Premier League table, but they can move into 14th place with victory on Friday night.

Eight teams - including Chelsea - possess a worse defensive record than Forest, emphasising the feeling that they could promptly move up the standings if they resolve their issues in the final third.

On the back of three defeats in four matches and with 20 goals conceded in 11 games, Chelsea will be perceived to be ideal opponents for Forest.

While Chelsea have the opportunity to move into fifth place, they are highly likely to end the weekend in the bottom half of the table should they lose in the East Midlands.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It has been revealed that it was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a fresh look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

Industry observers note that the 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Industry observers note that newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

It has been revealed that so Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline states. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”.

According to recent reports, good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Sources indicate that frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 26 Nov 2026 13:47.

Both beaten 5-1 last weekend, Frosinone and Parma will aim to bounce back when they clash at Stadio Benito Stirpe on Saturday.

Despite suffering consecutive defeats for the first time this term, the hosts are still 12 points above their visitors in the Serie A standings.

Frosinone made an unexpectedly strong start to their latest comeback campaign, scoring freely while winning six of their first 11 fixtures after returning to Serie A.

However, Massimiliano Alvini's attack-minded side then suffered a rare setback, going down 1-0 to Cagliari, before they were well beaten just after the international break.

Two goals down within 20 minutes, the Canarini continued to fly forward, but they never really recovered and ultimately lost 5-1 to AC Milan at San Siro.

In fact, Frosinone have only claimed two points on the road since beating Fiorentina at the end of August, so their form at Stadio Stirpe has kept them tucked inside the top half.

After narrowly losing their first home fixture against Juventus, they have since won all of the next five, so confidence should still be high when lowly Parma come to town.

While their promoted hosts sit seventh in Serie A, Parma are hovering above the relegation zone with just eight points on the board.

Like Frosinone, they were thumped 5-1 last week, as Roma stormed to victory at Stadio Tardini, with Capocannoniere leader Donyell Malen helping himself to four goals.

That was the Gialloblu's eighth defeat from their first 12 league games, and the recent hiring of their second-highest Serie A scorer has hardly had an impact.

Alberto Gilardino has only celebrated one win since succeeding Carlos Cuesta, who kept the Emilian club afloat last term, but that lone success did come on the road.

Following a run of six straight away defeats, Parma recently beat Atalanta 3-0 in Bergamo, so they will aim to claim more points when they head south on Saturday.

Now trailing Malen in the race to be crowned Italy's top scorer, Frosinone striker Antonio Raimondo is still sidelined by injury - and his deputy is also unavailable.

Daniel Birligea bagged a brace against Lecce before scoring for Romania in their recent Nations League camp, but he strained a hamstring in Milan and has been ruled out for the next few weeks.

So, it remains to be seen whether Alvini selects support forwards Fares Ghedjemis, Romano Schmid and Giorgi Kvernadze - each of whom have provided four Serie A assists - or Slovak centre-forward Tomas Bobcek to lead the hosts' attack.

On the absence front, Florian Grillitsch has yet to recover from a thigh problem, but left-back Gabriele Bracaglia can return after serving a one-match ban.

While Parma will welcome back Abdoulaye Ndiaye from suspension, Argentine striker David Romero is still ruled out by a serious shoulder injury; defensive duo Diego Carlos (thigh) and Dominik Drobnic (foot) are also doubts.

In Romero's absence, Simone Lontani could partner El Bilal Toure, but Nesta Elphege is also a contender after scoring the Gialloblu's lone goal against Roma.

Frosinone possible starting lineup:.

Palmisani; Oyono, Monterisi, Calvani, Bracaglia; Masini, Calo; Ghedjemis, Schmid, Kvernadze; Bobcek.

Parma possible starting lineup:.

Daffara; Delprato, Troilo, Ndiaye; Britschgi, Fabbian, Sierro, Keita, Valeri; Elphege, Toure.

Frosinone can arrest their decline with another home win, as Parma are in grim form and could face a long fight to avoid the drop.

Notably, the Canarini tend to start fast - scoring a league-high 11 goals inside the first 30 minutes - while their visitors have yet to score before the half-hour mark.

Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 58 min read (11519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~58 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood.
  • Sources indicate that shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8.
  • Recent findings suggest that forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres indicated more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

Sources indicate that shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8. Such redistribution can be characterized by shifts in tree abundance centres, which reveals how populations reorganize within their ranges2,9,10. Given that cooler conditions occur at higher latitudes and elevations, poleward and upslope shifts in species distribution are expected with climate change1,9,10,11,12. However, downslope shifts of tree species in montane ecosystems have also been reported, probably reflecting the influence of non-temperature factors that alter tree abundance and distribution in contrasting ways13,14,15,16. Natural disturbances, such as wildfires, diseases and insect outbreaks, along with subsequent regeneration, can alter stem abundance and basal area (the cross-sectional surface area of tree trunks measured at breast height—1.37 m above the ground) across regions4, influencing latitudinal or longitudinal shifts3. Yet, the roles of disturbances in shaping species’ elevational redistribution remains underexplored8.

Recent findings suggest that forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline. Over recent decades, these forests have experienced pronounced warming and frequent droughts17,18, which have increased wildfire activity19,20 and insect outbreaks21,22, and altered forest disease patterns22,23. As these disturbances can alter tree demographic dynamics4, elevational variation in disturbance activity may drive the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. Moreover, warming may shift disturbance patterns23,24,25, further influencing tree abundance redistribution. Although previous studies have reported elevational shifts across regions, most have been restricted geographically with inconsistent patterns9,14,26,27,28. A comprehensive and cross-regional assessment using a consistent methodology remains lacking, which limits our understanding of elevational shift patterns and their underlying mechanisms in the context of environmental change.

It has been revealed that to fill this gap, we quantified elevational shifts in tree abundance centres of common tree species across individual ecosections (ecoregion sections) in the western USA using remeasured plots conducted by the US Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) programme29. As the western USA spans a vast climatic and ecological gradient and encompasses diverse forest types, estimating elevational shifts across the entire region would mask regional-scale differences and could be confounded by species’ geographical redistribution among regions14,30,31,32. We therefore conducted our analyses separately within individual ecosections for each species. By selecting tree species that occurred in more than 100 remeasured FIA plots without evidence of silvicultural treatment within individual montane ecosections (Fig. 1a), we identified 45 species (Extended Data Table 1) across 33 ecosections, yielding 212 species–ecosection combinations. Collectively, they accounted for 68% of total stems and 69% of total basal area across montane forests in the western USA.

Sources indicate that in this study, we aimed to address three objectives: (1) to characterize patterns of elevational shifts in tree abundance centres across species–ecosections in the western USA under climate change and natural disturbances; (2) to examine how climate and disturbance jointly influence tree abundance changes and (3) to evaluate how elevational asymmetries in climate and disturbance activity influence the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. We quantified elevational shifts for individual species–ecosections using two measures of tree abundance: basal area and stem abundance. For each measure, the shift was calculated as the difference in species’ elevational centres between two inventory periods (T1, 1999–2013 and T2, 2012–2025), yielding the basal area shift and stem shift. Changes in stem abundance and basal area both reflect demographic processes but differ in their sensitivity to tree size classes. Stem abundance may be influenced more strongly by sapling dynamics (mortality and ingrowth), as saplings are typically more numerous than adult trees. Here, ingrowth refers to the entry of stems into a specified size class by crossing a diameter threshold as defined by the FIA: sapling ingrowth occurs when stems enter the 2.54–12.7 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) class, and adult ingrowth occurs when stems grow beyond 12.7 cm DBH. FIA ingrowth therefore represents the combined outcome of earlier recruitment, survival and growth sufficient for an individual to cross an inventory threshold. Basal area gives greater weight to larger trees and is influenced more strongly by the growth and mortality of adult trees. Thus, the two measures provide complementary information on population change. Because shifts in abundance centre ultimately arise from asymmetric tree abundance changes along species’ elevational gradients, understanding the drivers of plot-level tree abundance change is essential for interpreting the mechanisms underlying these shifts. We then assessed the effects of changes in mean annual temperature (MAT) and drought frequency, together with disturbance factors including fire, insect outbreaks and disease, on plot-level tree abundance changes. Finally, we investigated the elevational asymmetries in these environmental factors, defined as differences between elevational segments above (upper) and below (lower) the elevational centre at T1, and evaluated their associations with ecosection-level elevational shifts using generalized linear mixed models.

According to recent reports, elevational redistribution of basal area and stem abundance varied substantially among species–ecosections, with many showing little change in elevational centres whereas others exhibited significant upslope or downslope shifts (Extended Data Fig. 1). For basal area, shifts were more often downslope than upslope: 42 of 212 species–ecosections shifted significantly (P < 0.05) downslope and 28 shifted upslope, representing 30% and 11% of total basal area across all focal species–ecosections, respectively. When aggregating all species within individual ecosections, 12 of the total 33 ecosections shifted downslope, whereas four ecosections shifted upslope (Fig. 1c). Except for the Nevada–Utah Mountain Steppe (M341), downslope shifts were more common than upslope shifts across ecoregion provinces (Fig. 1c). When aggregating across ecosections by species, 16 species (61.5% total basal area) experienced a significant downslope shift and 11 (11.3% total basal area) shifted upslope. Among the eight most dominant species, six shifted downslope (P < 0.05), including Pseudotsuga menziesii (Douglas fir), Pinus ponderosa (ponderosa pine), Pinus contorta (lodgepole pine), Tsuga heterophylla (western hemlock), Picea engelmannii (Engelmann spruce) and Abies concolor (white fir), whereas none shifted upslope (Fig. 1d).

When measured by stem abundance, shift in elevational centre was more divergent. Specifically, 23 species–ecosections moved downslope and 22 upslope (Extended Data Fig. 1), representing 7.4% and 10.7% of total stem abundance across all focal species–ecosections, respectively (Fig. 1b). Spatially, five ecosections exhibited significant overall downslope shifts, whereas six ecosections revealed significant upslope shifts (Fig. 1c). At the species level, only three species shifted downslope and six shifted upslope (Fig. 1d), reflecting divergent elevational responses among ecosections within individual species (Extended Data Fig. 1).

In a recent development, to understand demographic changes underlying the observed elevational shifts, we examined range-edge dynamics by comparing relative tree abundance change between the upper and lower range segments for species–ecosections with significant shifts (Extended Data Fig. 2). Upper and lower range segments were defined as portions of a species’ range above and below the elevational centre weighted by basal area or stem abundance from the initial inventory (T1). For basal area, 61% of upslope shifts and 69% of downslope shifts were associated with consistent changes of basal area in upper and lower segments (either both declining or both increasing, but at differing rates above versus below the elevational centre). For stem abundance, 64% of upslope shifts were associated with declines at lower and increases at upper-range segments, whereas 57% of downslope shifts highlighted the opposite pattern. This indicates that stem shifts are associated with asymmetric demographic responses between cooler (upper) and warmer (lower) elevational segments, with increase in abundance at one end coupled with decline at the other.

According to recent reports, we further analysed the tree abundance change at upper and lower ranges for saplings and adult trees, separately. The asymmetric responses of saplings between range segments aligned with stem-based shifts, whereas those of adults aligned with basal area shifts, indicating that stem shifts were driven primarily by changes in sapling abundance and basal area shifts were driven primarily by changes in adult basal area (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Results were similar when using plots in the uppermost and lowermost 25% of elevations (Supplementary Fig. 1).

As uneven changes in tree abundance along elevational gradients drive shifts in abundance centre, we examined how plot-level changes in tree abundance were associated with climate change and disturbance history. From the recent past (1983–2002, as a baseline) to the study period (2003–2022), MAT in the study region increased by an average of 0.7 °C (Extended Data Fig. 3). Drought frequency, determined based on the 12-month Standardized Precipitation–Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) in July (SPEI12July), generally increased, with the largest increases in southern provinces. Based on FIA records, recent disturbances recorded at T2 (less than or equal to 10 years before revisit) and legacy disturbances recorded at T1 (10–15 years before revisit) revealed similar spatial patterns, but legacy disturbances affected smaller forest areas overall (Extended Data Fig. 4).

In a recent development, A generalized linear mixed model fitted across all species–ecosections revealed that climate, disturbance and their interactions were key drivers of stem abundance change (Fig. 2). Increases in temperature and drought frequency exerted modest but opposing influences on stem abundance: warming corresponded to gains, whereas greater drought frequency corresponded to losses. Baseline drought frequency partially mitigated the negative effects of increasing drought frequency on stem abundance, suggesting that forests historically exposed to more frequent droughts were more resistant to additional water stress.

a–f, Generalized linear mixed model coefficients are presented as percentage changes in stem abundance between inventories associated with a 1 s.d. increase in each predictor for all trees (a), saplings (c) and adults (e) (n = 74,448 samples for each analysis). Points, model coefficient estimates; error bars, 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All predictors except plant clade were standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before modelling; plant clade was included as a categorical predictor using sum-to-zero contrasts (angiosperm = 1, gymnosperm = −1). Positive coefficients (blue) indicate increases in stem abundance, whereas negative coefficients (red) indicate declines. Light grey shading is to distinguish three predictor categories (from top to bottom: climate, natural disturbances and others, which includes interactions between disturbances and climate variables or plant attributes). Predicted stem abundance responses to legacy fire extent for angiosperms and gymnosperms are shown for all trees (b), saplings (d) and adults (f). Solid lines, model-predicted mean percentage changes in stem abundance; shaded bands, 95% CIs. In the models, ΔMAT and ΔDrought represent changes in MAT and drought frequency, respectively, from the baseline (1983–2002) to the study (2003–2022) period; drought frequency is the number of years per decade with SPEI12July < −1.0. Fire, disease and insect variables indicate the proportion of forest area affected by each disturbance before T1 (legacy) or between T1 and T2 (recent). Statistical significance in a, c and e was assessed using two-sided Wald z-tests without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Significance levels are indicated as ***P < 0.001, **P < 0.01, *P < 0.05 and #P < 0.1. Exact P values are provided in the Source Data. Effects of the full model are provided in Extended Data Fig. 5.

Disturbances exerted strong effects on changes in stem abundance, and these effects differed between recent and legacy disturbances (Fig. 2). Recent fires were associated with the largest reductions in stem abundance, whereas legacy fires increased stem abundance, probably reflecting forest regeneration from earlier fires. Disease had generally weak effects, but legacy disease was associated with stronger negative effects than recent disease, suggesting more persistent impacts of earlier disease events. Conversely, recent insect outbreaks were associated with larger reductions in stem abundance than legacy outbreaks, consistent with partial recovery following earlier outbreaks. Moreover, where previous disease and insect outbreaks had occurred, recent fires were associated with greater declines in stem abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting interactive and compounding disturbance impacts.

In a recent development, fire effects also interacted with other factors including baseline drought, species’ fire tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm) (Fig. 2). Specifically, fires in historically dry areas were associated with smaller reductions in stem abundance, probably because lower vegetation productivity and fuel availability in dry forests can limit fire severity and associated mortality33. Recent fire effects also depended on species’ functional traits, with fire-tolerant species experiencing smaller declines following recent fires. Legacy fire was associated positively with stem abundance in both plant clades, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms (Fig. 2a,b). Despite some variation, models in individual provinces were largely consistent with the overall effects (Extended Data Fig. 6).

To evaluate potential life-stage differences in responses to environmental change, we also modelled stem abundance change separately for saplings and adult trees (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5). Warming primarily promoted sapling abundance but had little influence on adult abundance. Although recent fires consistently caused declines in both saplings and adults, legacy fires showed a positive effect on sapling abundance but a negative effect on adults. This indicates regeneration events after legacy fires, but many recruits are still below the 12.7 cm DBH threshold at plot remeasurement (10–15 years after fire). Disease decreased adult stem abundance; recent disease had little effect on saplings and legacy disease was associated with reduced sapling abundance. Legacy fire effects on stem abundance differed between saplings and adults, and between angiosperms and gymnosperms. Legacy fire was associated with increased stem abundance in saplings, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. By contrast, legacy fire slightly reduced adult stem abundance, with no significant difference observed between angiosperms and gymnosperms (Fig. 2d,f).

Models of basal area dynamics highlighted patterns similar to adult stem abundance (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8), reflecting a strong contribution of large trees to basal area. While MAT change had a marginally positive effect on basal area change (P = 0.056), drought frequency change and most disturbance factors showed negative effects, except for the non-significant effect of recent disease and positive effect of legacy fire. The positive effect of legacy fire was driven primarily by angiosperms, whereas gymnosperms showed relatively weak responses (Extended Data Fig. 7b,d).

To further understand the mechanisms underlying elevational shifts in tree abundance centres, we investigated how climate change and disturbance were distributed across species’ elevational gradients. We hypothesized that, rather than the average changes in environmental drivers across elevations, uneven exposure to the environmental changes between upper and lower range segments drives the observed elevational shifts in tree abundance centres. To test this hypothesis, we quantified differences in changes in climate (MAT and drought frequency) and disturbance extent between the two elevational segments (above and below the elevational centre at T1) for individual species–ecosections.

It has been revealed that overall, trees in upper-range segments experienced greater climate change and more extensive disturbance than in lower segments (Fig. 3). The upper–lower difference in the change in MAT (ΔMAT) was significantly positive for all the ecoregion provinces, indicating stronger warming at higher elevations (Fig. 3a). For drought frequency, lower range segments generally had higher values than upper segments during the baseline period (1983–2002), but this pattern partially reversed during the study period (2003–2022), with more ecoregion provinces showing higher drought frequency in upper segments (Supplementary Fig. 2). Consistent with this shift, temporal increases in drought frequency (ΔDrought) were greater in upper than lower species ranges in four ecoregion provinces, including Cascade Mixed Forest (M242), Sierran Steppe (M261), Arizona–Newly introduced Mexico Mountains Steppe (M313) and Northern Rocky Mountain Forest (M333) (Fig. 3b).

It has been revealed that patterns of disturbance asymmetry varied by type and period (Fig. 3c–h). Notably, recent fire and disease exhibited significantly (P < 0.05) positive upper–lower differences in more provinces than their legacy counterparts. Specifically, recent fires affected larger proportions of forest area in the upper range in three of the seven ecoregion provinces, whereas the lower range was more affected in only one province (Fig. 3f). By contrast, there was no clear evidence showing the elevational asymmetry in legacy fire. Recent disease affected larger upper-range proportions in three provinces (Fig. 3g), compared with two provinces for legacy disease (Fig. 3d). Both legacy and recent insect outbreaks were more prevalent in upper-range segments in three provinces.

Recent findings suggest that we then modelled elevational shift rate in basal area and stem abundance, with species–ecosections as observational units and upper–lower asymmetries in climate change and disturbance as predictors (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 9). For basal area shifts, upper–lower difference in recent fire extent and insect outbreak extent revealed significantly negative effects (P < 0.01), indicating that greater disturbance extents at one end of elevational range tended to displace population centres towards the opposite end. Elevational asymmetry in legacy fire showed a marginally significant positive effect on basal area shift on average (P = 0.053). The effect differed significantly between angiosperms and gymnosperms, with stronger upslope redistribution observed in angiosperms (Fig. 4a,b). Plant clade also showed a strong main effect, with angiosperms exhibiting more pronounced upslope shifts than gymnosperms under average covariate conditions across species–ecosections.

In a recent development, for stem shifts, upper–lower difference in ΔDrought, recent fire extent and legacy insect extent demonstrated negative effects. Asymmetric warming (ΔMAT) showed a positive but non-significant association with elevational shift (P = 0.19), implying that warming may promote upslope movement weakly but is probably overshadowed by disturbance and increasing drought frequency. Interaction effects further revealed that species with higher fire tolerance were less sensitive to elevational asymmetry of recent fire extent, consistent with trait-mediated resilience to disturbance. Elevational asymmetry in legacy fire extent also showed a positive effect, suggesting that a greater legacy fire extent at one end of the elevational range was associated with a shift of the elevational centre towards the same end, potentially reflecting post-fire regeneration within previously burned areas. This positive effect was marginally stronger in angiosperms than in gymnosperms (Fig. 4c,d). Similar to basal area shifts, the main effect of plant clade indicated that angiosperms generally exhibited more pronounced upslope shifts than gymnosperms.

Across 212 species–ecosection combinations spanning broad climatic and biogeographical gradients in the western USA, many tree abundance centres remained relatively stable despite ongoing climate change and natural disturbance. This relative stability probably reflected opposing demographic processes, with ingrowth and growth promoted by warming and post-disturbance recovery counterbalanced by mortality associated with drought and disturbance. Where redistribution occurred, stem shifts were divergent, whereas basal area shifts were more commonly downslope (Fig. 1). Stem abundance is influenced more strongly by sapling ingrowth, whereas basal area is linked more closely to larger tree dynamics. The discrepancy between stem and basal area shifts suggests a general upslope redistribution of smaller trees relative to larger trees, consistent with previous findings that seedlings tend to occupy higher elevations than adults28. Elevational shifts in tree abundance centre arise from asymmetric changes in abundance along species’ elevational gradients (Extended Data Fig. 2) and therefore reflect demographic redistribution within species ranges in response to environment change.

Industry observers note that our findings demonstrate that both climate change and natural disturbances, along with their interactions, are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics across the forests of the western USA. The strong negative effects of increasing drought frequency align with extensive evidence of drought-induced mortality and reduced growth under water stress34,35,36. In historically drought-prone areas, drought effects on stem abundance were weaker, consistent with evidence that previous or recurrent drought may enhance resistance to subsequent water stress through stress-memory mechanisms37. This pattern was more evident for sapling abundance than for adult stem abundance, suggesting that drought history may alter the balance between sapling mortality and sapling ingrowth more strongly. By contrast, warming exhibited positive effects on stem abundance, driven largely by enhanced sapling ingrowth or reduced sapling mortality (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5). This pattern suggests that temperature increases can promote regeneration where moisture remains sufficient38, which often occurs in cooler or higher-elevation sites.

Industry observers note that although fires, disease and insect outbreaks all reduce tree abundance, their effects unfold differently over time. Biotic disturbances such as disease and insect outbreaks caused prolonged declines, as pathogens and pests can persist for years and continue to kill trees39. By contrast, fires triggered abrupt losses in tree abundance followed by gradual increases during post-fire recovery and regeneration40. Our comparison of recent and legacy disturbances is limited to events recorded by the FIA annual inventory, which captures only a relatively recent disturbance history before plot remeasurement. Because post-disturbance recovery can unfold over longer time scales, earlier events not recorded in the FIA disturbance history may also have contributed to tree abundance redistribution but could not be evaluated directly in our analysis.

It has been revealed that post-fire regeneration has an key role in changing stem abundance and elevational distributions, but its effects differed markedly between angiosperms and gymnosperms (Fig. 2). The relatively weak responses of gymnosperms to legacy fires are consistent with recent studies reporting widespread post-fire regeneration failure of gymnosperms in warm, dry and often low-elevation forests in the western USA41,42. When regeneration thresholds are crossed, fire can act as a tipping point: instead of returning to closed-canopy forest, sites may transition to shrubland, grassland or sparse woodland. By contrast, angiosperms showed relatively stronger positive responses to legacy fire, which aligns with the greater capacity for vegetative resprouting of many angiosperms following fires43. Such contrasting post-fire responses suggest that fires may increasingly promote divergent elevational redistribution between angiosperms and gymnosperms.

In a recent development, although climate change and disturbance pressures drive tree abundance changes, their elevational asymmetry (differences between upper and lower range segments) emerged as an crucial predictor of the direction and magnitude of species’ elevational shifts (Fig. 4). Processes that reduce tree abundance including increasing drought frequency and recent disturbances can shift population centres away from the affected end of a species’ elevational range, whereas processes that enhance tree abundance such as warming and post-disturbance recovery at one end pull population centres towards the affected end. Under natural disturbance, stronger pressures in upper-range segments across the western USA (Fig. 3) were associated with more frequent downslope shifts in basal area. When plots affected by silvicultural treatments were included, however, basal area shifts were distributed more evenly between upslope and downslope directions (Supplementary Fig. 5), possibly reflecting the greater prevalence of timber harvest at lower elevations8. These results suggest that the elevational distributions can be modified by other elevationally asymmetric influences, including human activities. By explicitly quantifying these asymmetric environmental pressures rather than relying on area-averaged climate trends and disturbance, our approach captures the spatial heterogeneity that shapes demographic processes directly at species’ range segments. Although conceptually intuitive, such asymmetry has rarely been incorporated explicitly into broad-scale assessments of species redistribution. Our findings highlight the need to consider not only regional trends in climate and disturbance, but also how these pressures are distributed across elevation gradients.

Overall, natural disturbances and drought had stronger effects than warming in our models, probably reflecting differences in the time scales of demographic processes, including mortality, ingrowth and growth. Although natural disturbances and drought can reduce tree abundance rapidly through mortality, increases in stem abundance through ingrowth and in basal area through growth accumulate over time. Given the relatively short remeasurement interval (approximately 10 years) in this study, sapling ingrowth may be more evident than adult ingrowth, which may partly explain why adult stem abundance was less sensitive to warming and legacy disturbance than sapling abundance42. These differences in temporal sensitivity may also contribute to the different patterns of stem and basal area shifts. Basal area shifts, which are dominated by larger trees, were more commonly downslope and associated with greater disturbance activity in upper-range segments (Fig. 3). By contrast, stem shifts were more divergent, probably because sapling ingrowth can offset mortality losses more rapidly in smaller trees. Similar demographic differences may also underlie the contrasting redistribution patterns between plant clades. Angiosperms, which generally exhibit stronger recruitment and post-disturbance recovery43, highlighted greater upslope redistribution than gymnosperms (Fig. 4b,d). This underscores the importance of long-term monitoring, as repeated measurements over longer intervals are essential for capturing the full demographic imprint of sustained warming and disturbance on species redistribution.

Climate change may have exerted indirect effects on forest redistribution by altering disturbance regimes and their elevational distributions19,44,45. Although lower elevations in forests in the western USA were generally drier than higher elevations during the baseline period (1983–2002), drought frequency has increased disproportionately in upper-range segments in recent decades (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2). This increase in drought frequency, together with stronger warming in species’ upper-range segments, may help explain the greater fire activity observed there23,24,46. Consistent with our findings, wildfires in the western USA have advanced upslope at an average rate of 7.6 m per year between 1984 and 2017 (ref. 24). Moreover, elevated winter temperatures have enabled mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae) to survive at higher elevations than previously possible, exposing previously less affected high-elevation forests to greater pest pressure47.

In a recent development, our study underscores the substantial influence of disturbances, particularly wildfires and insect outbreaks, on tree abundance and elevational redistribution. Recent disturbances were often associated with reduced tree abundance, driving abundance centres shifting downslope. Meanwhile, climate warming and post-fire recovery tended to increase tree abundance, and post-fire recovery was associated with upslope shifts in tree abundance centres. Therefore, the combined pressures from climate change and disturbances place forest ecosystems in the western USA ‘between a rock and a hard place’. Given projected future climate change and increasing disturbance activities globally45, our findings highlight the need for continued monitoring and adaptive forest management strategies to mitigate these impacts and promote ecosystem sustainability and resilience.

Industry observers note that the annual inventory of the FIA programme uses a nationally consistent plot design (around 1 plot per 2,428 hectares (ha)) and provides remeasurements with consistent data collection procedures nationwide, enabling robust estimation of changes in forest structure and species distribution. Each FIA plot consists of four 168 m2 subplots on which adult trees (DBH ≥ 12.7 cm) are measured. Within each subplot, a 13.5 m2 microplot is nested to sample saplings (2.54 cm ≤ DBH < 12.7 cm)29. For some plots, additional macroplots are established to measure very large trees. To account for differences in sampling area among microplots, subplots and macroplots, we used the trees-per-acre expansion factors provided by FIA, which standardize tree abundance estimates to a common per-area basis. We obtained forest attributes from the initial inventory period (T1, 1999–2013) and the subsequent remeasurement period (T2, 2012–2025). Because forest management can influence regional patterns of tree density, we excluded plots that showed evidence of recent silvicultural activity, including harvesting, artificial regeneration or site preparation. A total of 44,368 forest plots located within montane ecoregions were selected across 11 western US states (Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, California, Utah, Nevada, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico). The average interval between measurements was approximately 10 years.

It has been revealed that elevational shifts were quantified within individual species–ecosection combinations, rather than across the entire western US, to avoid conflating elevational shifts with latitudinal shifts. Ecoregion boundaries followed the US Forest Service 2007 ecoregion map48. We selected 45 tree species that occurred in more than 100 remeasured FIA plots without evidence of silvicultural treatment within individual montane ecosections, yielding 212 species–ecosection combinations across 33 ecosections. For each species–ecosection, elevational shifts were quantified as the difference in the stem abundance-weighted or basal area-weighted elevational centres of all trees (DBH ≥ 2.54 cm) between the two inventory periods. The shift rate (metres per decade) was calculated by dividing the elevational shift distance by the mean remeasurement interval of plots where the target species was present. To examine spatial and taxonomic patterns, we further aggregated species–ecosection elevational shifts to the ecosection and species levels. For stem shifts, the mean shift for each aggregation was calculated using stem abundance as a weighting factor, whereas basal area was used as the weight for basal area shifts.

Because ecosection boundaries can intersect species’ elevational ranges, particularly at lower elevations, they may influence the observed elevational shifts by truncating portions of species distributions. To evaluate the potential impact of this boundary effect, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by extending montane ecosections into adjacent non-montane regions using spatial buffers. We applied buffer widths of 50 km and 100 km, which correspond roughly to the average width of counties in the western USA and are appropriate given the spatial uncertainty associated with FIA plot coordinate swapping within counties. Elevational shifts were recalculated under each buffering scenario and compared with the original estimates based on unbuffered ecosections. The overall distribution of elevational shifts remained highly consistent among the 0 km, 50 km and 100 km buffering scenarios (Supplementary Fig. 6). Therefore, we retained the original Bailey’s ecosections as the primary study units because buffering produced little change in the overall patterns.

This study aimed to examine how natural processes, including climate change and natural disturbances, influence tree elevational redistribution in montane forests in the western USA. Because silvicultural treatments often depend on local management objectives, ownership and socioeconomic conditions, we excluded plots that showed evidence of recent silvicultural activity from the main analysis. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the elevational shift calculations with these plots included. This analysis produced more upslope shifts in basal area centres than the treatment-excluded analysis, resulting in a more balanced number of upslope and downslope shifts (Supplementary Fig. 5), possibly reflecting low-elevation timber harvest8. We therefore focused on the treatment-excluded analysis to minimize the influence of silvicultural treatments and better evaluate tree redistribution associated primarily with climate change and natural disturbances.

Sources indicate that to test whether the observed shifts in elevational centre were statistically significant, we used a non-parametric bootstrap resampling approach3,49,50. For each species–ecosection combination, FIA plots were treated as the resampling unit, and paired T1 and T2 observations were resampled together with replacement using the original sample size (Supplementary Table 1). In each iteration, elevational centres for both inventory periods and the resulting elevational shift were recalculated. This procedure was repeated 10,000 times to generate a bootstrap distribution of elevational shift estimates. From the distribution, we derived percentile-based 95% CIs and corresponding empirical two-tailed P values. A shift was considered significant when the 95% CI did not include zero. The two-tailed P value was calculated as twice the smaller proportion of bootstrap estimates greater or less than 0, representing the probability of observing a shift as extreme as the empirical value under the null hypothesis of no change.

In the FIA, plots are divided into conditions representing distinct landscape units based on attributes identified by field crews, such as ownership, land type (for example, forest, water) and evidence of disturbance. The proportional area of each condition within a plot is recorded. The FIA database records disturbance events on mapped forest conditions, such as fire, insect outbreak and disease, that occurred since the last measurement in a remeasurement or within the last 5 years for upcoming plots. Only disturbance events affecting at least 1 acre (0.4 ha) in size (including both the plot and adjacent affected areas) and causing mortality or damage to at least 25% of trees were recorded51. Based on the recorded condition proportions, we calculated the total forest area and that disturbed by any of the three principal disturbance agents including fire, insect outbreak and disease in each plot at both the initial inventory (T1; legacy) and remeasured inventory (T2; recent). On average, legacy and recent fires occurred 13.1 and 4.1 years before the T2 remeasurement, respectively. Note that one plot could experience more than one type of disturbance agent, and the area was attributed to each agent based on its specific disturbance, resulting in possible overlap among disturbance agents. For each species–ecosection, we summed forest area and disturbed area from plots using FIA-defined expansion factors with the target species present and calculated the disturbance extent as the proportion of disturbed forest area to the total forest area at both inventories.

For climate variables, we used 800-m resolution monthly temperature data from the PRISM Climate Group Long-Term dataset52 (https://data.prism.oregonstate.edu/time_series/us/lt/800m/) and 4-km SPEI12July from the WestWide Drought Tracker53 (https://wrcc.app/climate/wwdt/archives). The PRISM long-term dataset was used because it is based only on long-term stations of record and is therefore considered more temporally stable than the PRISM All-Network dataset54. SPEI is a drought index calculated as difference between precipitation and potential evapotranspiration over a specified time period55. SPEI12July was used because it is correlated strongly with tree mortality and growth56,57,58,59,60. Drought events were determined as years with SPEI12July < −1.0 (refs. 57,58,61,62,63,64). MAT and drought frequency (number of drought years per decade) were calculated in the recent past (1983–2002) for a baseline and the study period (2003–2022). Climate change was calculated as the difference between these two periods, accounting for potential lags between climatic trends and vegetation responses1,65. For each species–ecosection, climate variables were extracted from all plots where the species occurred and averaged to obtain ecosection-level estimates.

True FIA plot coordinates are not released publicly to ensure ecological integrity and protect landowner privacy. Instead, the publicly available FIA data apply a ‘fuzzing and swapping’ protocol. On public lands, plot locations are displaced randomly, typically by less than 0.8 km and rarely up to 1.6 km. For private lands, up to 20% of plots are swapped with another plot of similar attributes within the same county. Although these procedures introduce spatial uncertainty, their influence on our analyses is expected to be negligible for several reasons. First, plot elevation in the FIA data is generally accurate, and our analysis of elevational shifts relies on repeated measurements of the same plots, for which elevation remains constant across inventories. Second, around 76% of the plots used in this study occur on public lands with location offsets (<0.8 km). Although these offsets may introduce climate uncertainty because elevation and vegetation types can vary substantially within a single 0.8- or 4-km pixel, such mismatches are expected to be largely random across the large number of FIA plots (44,368) and therefore have limited influence on the overall conclusions of this study. Finally, for private plots, the swapping process pairs plots with similar forest type, stand size, latitude and longitude, ensuring that local climatic and ecological conditions remain comparable.

We computed elevational asymmetry for relative tree abundance change (Extended Data Fig. 2), climate change and disturbance extent (Fig. 3) by calculating their difference between upper and lower range segments. Relative tree abundance change between T1 and T2 was quantified for stem abundance and basal area as a symmetric percent change, which places increase and decreases on a common scale (the average of T1 and T2) and avoids the asymmetry of conventional percent change66. Upper and lower range segments are defined as the elevational range above and below the elevational centre weighted by stem abundance or basal area from the initial inventory (T1). We also conducted analysis using plots within the uppermost and lowermost 25% of elevations and found similar patterns (Supplementary Figs. 1, 3 and 4).

Species attributes of fire tolerance, drought tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm) were obtained from the US Department of Agriculture PLANTS Database (https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/). In PLANTS, fire tolerance qualitatively describes a species’ ability to survive or recover from fire and is classified into four levels: None, Low, Medium and High. Similarly, drought tolerance, describing a species’ ability to survive or maintain function under low soil moisture, is categorized into three levels: Low, Medium and High. For the four species lacking trait entries in PLANTS (Juniperus deppeana, Quercus arizonica, Quercus wislizeni and Quercus grisea), tolerance classes were assigned on the basis of expert knowledge. Detailed information on species attributes is provided in Extended Data Table 1.

We used a non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test to evaluate whether the upper–lower differences in climate change and disturbance extent were significantly different from zero (Fig. 2). We modelled the plot-level change in stem abundance and basal area between inventories using the log response ratio (LRR):.

Industry observers note that where \({M}_{T1}\) and \({M}_{T2}\) denote the values of stem abundance or basal area measured at T1 and T2, respectively, and c is a small pseudocount (set to 0.5 in this study) to avoid division by zero. Models were fitted in R using the glmmTMB67 package (v.1.1.10) with a Gaussian error distribution and identity link. Fixed effects included baseline climate and climate changes for MAT and drought frequency derived from SPEI12July, disturbance extents by fire, disease and insects during T1 (legacy) and T2 (recent), and species attributes including fire tolerance, drought tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm). We also included interactions between baseline climate and climate changes, between baseline drought frequency and recent disturbance extent, and between disturbance and species attributes. Fire and drought tolerance classes were converted to continuous variables to facilitate model fitting. Plant clade was included as a categorical predictor using sum-to-zero contrasts (angiosperm = 1, gymnosperm = −1). All predictors except plant clade are standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before modelling. Species and ecosection were included as random effects. Because the models included several interaction terms (for example, climate change versus baseline climate), we evaluated collinearity among predictors using variance inflation factor. All predictors variance inflation factors less than 5, indicating acceptable collinearity, and no variables were excluded from the final models. For interpretability, model coefficients and their 95% CIs were later back-transformed from the log response ratio as \(100\times [{e}^{\beta }-1]\) and expressed as percentage changes in tree abundance associated with a 1 s.d. increase in each continuous predictor. Models were fitted for all plots across species–ecosections, separately for each ecoregion province, and for saplings and adult trees. The full models are provided in Extended Data Figs. 5 and 8.

It has been revealed that elevational shifts in stem abundance and basal area of species–ecosections were also modelled using glmmTMB with Gaussian error distribution and identity link. Predictors included the upper–lower difference in climate change, disturbance extent and their interactions (Extended Data Fig. 9). Species identity was included as a random effect. We also evaluated ecoregion province as an additional random intercept, but its variance was negligible and it had little influence on model results. Therefore, only species identity was retained in the final models.

Industry News: Jude Bellingham scores 'the best goal of my life' as his stunning long-range volley helps Real Madrid come from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in the Champions League

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 18:45 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Jude Bellingham underlined his class once more with a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
  • With Real trailing 1-0 at half-time, the England superstar - who started as a substitute to rest - was one of three changes made by Jose Mourinho and his impact was felt 15 minutes later in an emphatic style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 18:45 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 25 November 2026.

Jude Bellingham underlined his class once more with a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

With Real trailing 1-0 at half-time, the England superstar - who started as a substitute to rest - was one of three changes made by Jose Mourinho and his impact was felt 15 minutes later in an emphatic style.

Collecting a loose ball from around 25 yards outside the box, Bellingham controlled it with his left foot, before flicking it up with his right foot and volleying it with the outside of that boot into the far corner of the PSV goal. The pace and precision of the strike was breathtaking as it flew past Matej Kovar and hit the inside of the post before going in.

It was a strike that was befitting of any match, and it proved to be the decisive one as that made it 2-1 to the hosts before they later ran riot.

Speaking post-match, Bellingham was clear where he ranked that finish, declaring: 'I think this was the best goal of my life.'.

He later elaborated to TNT Sports about his goal: 'They're [his goals] normally a lot closer, aren't they,' he joked.

SENSATIONAL JUDE BELLINGHAM 🤯Bellingham gives the hosts the lead with a magnificent volley 🔥 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/WdP6ULx8wE.

Jude Bellingham (right) scored a stunning volley to inspire Real Madrid to beat PSV Eindhoven.

Bellingham came off the bench to put Real ahead with this beautiful right-footed volley.

PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar could only watch on as the ball flew past him and go into the net.

'That one was a nice one, it popped up for me nicely and I just thought I'd hit it with the outside of my boot.

'I'm not one for smashing the ball too hard and it was a nice moment and important for the win as well.'.

Bellingham's performance, he also set up Vinicius Jr for the fifth goal, was acknowledged by Mourinho and Real captain Fede Valverde, who scored their equaliser, post-match too.

Industry observers note that 'Obviously Jude is a different type of player and he gave us what we didn't have in the first half,' Mourinho said. 'He changed the game, scored an incredible goal.'.

According to recent reports, valverde concurred declaring: 'He did well. We were struggling to keep the ball behind their midfielders and when Jude came in he gave us that tranquillity to control possession.'.

The strike comes a day after Daily Mail Sport reported that the 23-year-old is in advance talks over a fresh Real Madrid contract that will make him one of the best-paid players in Europe.

Madrid have been eager to tie down the in-form England midfielder beyond his current contract, understood to be worth around £12.5million a year after tax, which runs until 2029, in recognition of his performances.

Talks were initiated in September over an extension until 2031 and have been progressing well since with sources at Madrid confident they are close to reaching a conclusion.

Bellingham is in advance contract talks with Real Madrid over signing an extension until 2031.

Bellingham is expected to be handed improved terms to put him on par with team-mate Vinicius Jr, who agreed a new deal last summer reputedly on around £500,000 a week after tax.

As for Tuesday's win over PSV, Real are now top of the Champions League league phase standings after maintaining their 100 per cent record in the competition this season with a fifth-straight win.

According to recent reports, 1. Erling Haaland, Manchester City: £510,000 per week.

It has been revealed that 2. Kylian Mbappe, Real Madrid: £503,000 per week.

3. Vinicius Jr, Real Madrid: £500,000 per week.

According to recent reports, 4. Harry Kane, Bayern Munich: £402,000 per week.

Sources indicate that 5. Virgil van Dijk, Liverpool: £350,000 per week.

However, they didn't have it all their own way as PSV took a deserved lead in the 32nd minute from the penalty spot, with 37-year-old captain Ivan Perisic showing all his experience, ignoring the whistles ringing out around the Bernabeu before sending Thibaut Courtois the wrong way.

They almost doubled their lead before the break as the unmarked Kodai Sano glanced a header off target as the visitors continued to cause Real serious problems.

Real equalised five minutes after the break, thanks to Arda Guler's quick-thinking, with the Turkish midfielder flicking a backheeled pass to Valverde in the area, who steered his first-time shot into the bottom corner.

Real's fans were on their feet 10 minutes later, scarcely believing what they had seen, while Bellingham's team-mates looked similarly shell-shocked.

Marc Cucurella walked away with his head in his hands in wonder while the other Real players rushed to congratulate the scorer.

Real took command after Bellingham's goal and punished a loose pass in the PSV defence, Guler finding the unmarked Mbappe to extend the France forward's scoring run to seven successive Champions League appearances.

Mbappe added his second before Vinicius rounded off a resounding victory from Bellingham's pass, underlining the Spanish side's credentials as serious contenders to take Paris Saint-Germain's crown.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 13:52.
  • Aiming to remain unbeaten at home in the league this season, promotion-hunting Birmingham City host struggling Bolton Wanderers at St Andrew's @ Knighthead Park in the Championship on Saturday afternoon.
  • Blues were the latest side to take advantage of Burnley's Turf Moor misery on Wednesday night, whilst the Wanderers suffered defeat on their own patch by West Bromwich Albion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 13:52.

Aiming to remain unbeaten at home in the league this season, promotion-hunting Birmingham City host struggling Bolton Wanderers at St Andrew's @ Knighthead Park in the Championship on Saturday afternoon.

Blues were the latest side to take advantage of Burnley's Turf Moor misery on Wednesday night, whilst the Wanderers suffered defeat on their own patch by West Bromwich Albion.

As has been the case after each of their three Championship defeats so far this season, Birmingham City bounced back from last weekend's Stoke City disappointment by claiming three points, this time at the expense of crisis-hit Burnley.

Chris Davies's side have already equalled the number of away victories that they managed across the entirety of last season (6) courtesy of August Priske's seventh league goal of the term and an own goal from Clarets winger Jaydon Banel at Turf Moor.

Following seven wins from their past nine second-tier contests, Birmingham are occupying fourth position in the Championship table, three points behind current pacesetters Middlesbrough and Stoke.

Apart from a 6-1 battering by Brentford in the EFL Cup, Blues have been impressive at St Andrew's this season, with Saturday's hosts unbeaten across their opening eight home league battles (W4 D4).

In fact, Birmingham last experienced Second City defeat in the Championship at the beginning of April, and Davies has lost just three home league games since taking charge during the summer of 2024.

Sliding towards the relegation zone, Bolton Wanderers have now won just one of their past seven Championship contests (D2 L4) after losing to West Brom at the Toughsheet Community Stadium earlier in the week.

A second-half penalty from Ruben Rodrigues levelled the scores momentarily following Albion's opener, however, further strikes from Norwegian duo Aune Heggebo and Felix Horn Myhre sentenced the Wanderers to a fourth defeat in their past six games.

Winless in their past five games (D1 L4) at the Toughsheet, Bolton's last three victories have all arrived on the road, with Saturday's underdog visitors beating Norwich City (4-3), Wolverhampton Wanderers (3-1) and Charlton Athletic (1-0) since late September.

There is no doubting that the newly-promoted side are one of the favourites to suffer relegation this season, with Steven Schumacher's troops at the moment six points clear of the bottom three.

Bolton were defeated on their most recent trip to St Andrew's in October 2024 but were one of only three teams to beat Birmingham during their record-breaking League One title romp of 2024-25.

Birmingham City Championship form:.

Bolton Wanderers Championship form:.

Birmingham defender Ethan Laird missed the Burnley win after picking up a knock at Stoke last weekend, with the right-back a doubt for the Second City match on Saturday.

As a result, Bright Osayi-Samuel is likely to retain his spot in defence, with Dael Fry set to drop out in order to make room for the available-again Christoph Klarer.

Liam Millar, Jhon Solis and Jay Stansfield were rested for the final 15 minutes at Turf Moor, with the trio all set to start once again this weekend.

There is likely to be alteration on the right flank, though, where Patrick Roberts could be the key to unlocking a deep Bolton block.

Bolton rotated leading marksman Sam Dalby out of the starting side on Wednesday but the Englishman is fully expected to return to the XI on Saturday.

Ben Davies could feature against his former loan employers, whilst Samuel Illing-Junior is in line for another start following a bright display against West Brom.

Beadle; Osayi-Samuel, Neumann, Klarer, Cochrane; Iwata, Solis; Roberts, Stansfield, Millar; Priske.

Bolton Wanderers possible starting lineup:.

Bazunu; Stephenson, Brunt, Forino-Joseph, Conway; Simons, Sheehan; Larrazabal, Ito, Illing-Junior; Dalby.

After winning four straight home matches by an aggregate scoreline of 12-1, Birmingham are the overwhelming favourites for another Second City success this weekend.

Bolton have recent experience of producing a shock result in the West Midlands, however, we feel that Davies's St Andrew's juggernaut will be too strong in this matchup.

By Matthew Cooper | 26 Nov 2026 13:53, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 13:53.

Wigan Athletic will be looking to continue their good form when they welcome Plymouth Argyle to the Brick Community Stadium on Saturday.

The hosts at the moment sit 17th in the League One table, while the visitors are eighth.

Wigan could pick up a fifth consecutive victory this weekend, having found their form in recent weeks.

After suffering four defeats in five games last month, Wigan have won five of their last six across all competitions and are unbeaten in their last four league matches.

The Latics beat managerless Blackpool 2-1 last weekend, coming from behind to earn a crucial three points thanks to goals from Jon Mellish and Finley Burns.

The result leaves Gary Caldwell's side 17th with 17 points from 16 matches, with their recent uptick in form moving them four points clear of the relegation zone.

It is also worth noting that Wigan have only lost once to Plymouth in their last eight meetings across all competitions, although that defeat was a 3-0 loss that came last season.

Plymouth, meanwhile, have endured a difficult few weeks as they back-to-back defeats in the league without scoring.

Tom Cleverley's side were beaten 3-0 away to Sheffield Wednesday before losing 2-0 at home to Peterborough United.

In fact, Plymouth have won just one of their last six league games and will be keen to get back winning ways on Saturday.

The Pilgrims remain just three points off the playoffs and Cleverley has urged his injury-hit side to "really work hard to improve".

Wigan are expected to stick with the same side that beat Blackpool, with Scott Hogan set to lead the line ahead of Jensen Weir and Bradley Burrowes.

Max Power and Ryan Trevitt should continue in midfield, with Fraser Murray and Mellish set to feature out wide.

Plymouth are set to be without the likes of Bim Pepple, Joe Edwards, Owen Oseni, Michael Baidoo, Julio Plequezuelo and Alex Mitchell through injury.

Will Evans and Caleb Watts are expected to start up front, with Xavier Amaechi and Ronan Curtis providing support out wide.

Wigan Athletic possible starting lineup:.

Whitworth; Burns, Carragher, Fox; Murray, Power, Trevitt, Mellish; Weir, Burrowes; Hogan.

Plymouth Argyle possible starting lineup:.

Cooper; Harding, Ross, Hartridge, MacKenzie; Amaechi, Boateng, White, Curtis; Evans, Watts.

PSV Eindhoven vs. Go Ahead Eagles - prediction, team news, lineups

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 14:12.
  • Looking to move on from their midweek Champions League collapse against Real Madrid, PSV Eindhoven return to the bread and butter of Eredivisie football on Saturday.
  • The defending champions welcome Go Ahead Eagles to the Philips Stadion in gameweek 14, seeking a response to their humbling experience in the Spanish capital as they chase a fourth consecutive top-flight victory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 14:12.

Looking to move on from their midweek Champions League collapse against Real Madrid, PSV Eindhoven return to the bread and butter of Eredivisie football on Saturday.

The defending champions welcome Go Ahead Eagles to the Philips Stadion in gameweek 14, seeking a response to their humbling experience in the Spanish capital as they chase a fourth consecutive top-flight victory.

An Ivan Perisic goal made things interesting at the Bernabeu in midweek, but a Jude Bellingham-inspired second-half performance saw Jose Mourinho's Los Blancos run riot and eventually claim a 5-1 victory over PSV.

That loss, the Dutch giants' third in five European matches, leaves them 30th in the 36-team league-phase standings and their top-eight prospects looking increasingly remote.

However, Peter Bosz's men remain in contention for the qualification playoffs, with 24th-placed Villarreal just two points ahead of the reigning Eredivisie champions.

The Farmers will undoubtedly welcome a return to home comforts on Saturday as they seek to regain winning momentum after their chastening experience in the Spanish capital.

League football has brought greater encouragement, particularly in recent weeks, with three consecutive victories following a run of one win in four matches between late September and late October.

Scoring at least four goals in each of their victories over Willem II (7-0), Cambuur (6-2) and NEC (4-1) suggests a return to their free-scoring best, boding well for this weekend's visit from Go Ahead Eagles.

The Deventer outfit travel to Eindhoven in indifferent form, with a 1-0 away victory over SBV Excelsior coming between defeats to Cambuur and Fortuna Sittard.

Particularly notable has been the attacking decline of Joseph Oosting's men, who have scored just once across their last three league matches after averaging 2.3 goals per game over the opening 10 gameweeks.

While that sample remains too small for firm conclusions, the Pride of the IJssel's dip cannot be dismissed ahead of their trip to the Philips Stadion, where Kowet claimed a stunning 2-1 KNVB Beker semi-final victory in February 2025 en route to lifting their first domestic cup.

Paul Simonis was in charge for that historic success as Go Ahead Eagles secured their first victory in Eindhoven for 57 years, and they now seek a first Eredivisie win at PSV since 1968.

That will be easier mentioned than done, however, as their historical struggles and recent scoring decline leave them vulnerable against hosts still reeling from their Santiago Bernabeu beatdown.

PSV Eindhoven form (all competitions):.

Go Ahead Eagles Eredivisie form:.

Go Ahead Eagles form (all competitions):.

Mauro Junior (groin), Sami Ouaissa (muscle), Adamo Nagalo, Alassane Plea and Jerdy Schouten (ACL) remain unavailable for PSV; however, Ricardo Pepi should feature in some capacity after remaining on the bench in Madrid.

No player has scored more Eredivisie goals than Sven Mijnans, with the versatile attacking midfielder registering nine strikes and three assists in the top flight.

Guus Til is likely to lead the attack despite Pepi's availability, while Ruben van Bommel offers a dual threat after contributing five goals and three assists.

Soren Tengstedt shares Mijnans's position atop the league's scoring charts, with no player outscoring the Kowet forward this season.

Stefan Ingi Sigurdarson (four goals, one assist) and Mathis Suray (three goals, four assists) also possess match-winning quality that Oosting will hope comes to the fore at the Philips Stadion.

Go Ahead Eagles remain without Pim Saathof (ACL), while Evert Linthorst and Dean James will be assessed closer to kick-off.

PSV Eindhoven possible starting lineup:.

Kovar; Dest, Geertruida, Obispo, Kostic; Sano, Fernandez; Perisic, Mijnans, Van Bommel; Til.

Go Ahead Eagles possible starting lineup:.

Cillessen; Sampsted, Dirksen, Kramer, Baeten; Meulensteen, Rahmouni; Tengstedt, Edvardsen, Suray; Sigurdarson.

PSV's collapse in Madrid exposed their limitations in Europe, but scoring 17 goals across their last three Eredivisie victories underlines the different challenge they present domestically.

Go Ahead Eagles have managed just one goal in their last three league matches, and the hosts have our backing to deliver a convincing response at the Philips Stadion.
